newsitem.title: CHINA: HK faces challenges over legislature, poll plans.
newsitem.headline: HK faces challenges over legislature, poll plans.

text.p: Hong Kong's new China-backed leaders, now in their second month in office, are facing ever louder criticism and challenges over the new, unelected legislature and their plans for 1998 legislative polls.
Pro-democracy activist Emily Lau on Sunday blasted last week's appeal court ruling that crushed a challenge to the legality of the provisional legislature installed by Beijing.

In a decision that averted a constitutional crisis, the court ruled that local courts had no power to rule on the legality of the assembly because it had been appointed by China's parliament, the National People's Congress (NPC).

"By declaring the SAR (Special Administrative Region) court's inability to challenge the legality of decisions made by the NPC, the court of appeal is effectively saying that the NPC can do whatever it wants despite stipulations in the Basic Law," Lau, a former elected legislator, said in a radio programme.
The Basic Law is the Beijing-designed constitution for Hong Kong, which took effect the moment the former British colony returned to Chinese rule on July 1.

"The Basic Law even limits the authority of the NPC in the Hong Kong Special Administrative Region. However, under the scenario envisaged by the Court of Appeal, one cannot help but ask why the Basic Law has been promulgated at all," Lau said.
On taking over Hong Kong, Beijing scrapped the elected colonial legislature and replaced it with the appointed chamber which it intends should operate until a new legislature is elected next year.
But the unelected interim body, condemned by democrats as lacking legal basis, is facing a spate of fresh challenges.

The Democratic Party, headed by the outspoken Martin Lee, pledged on Sunday to offer free legal services to groups challenging the chamber, which recently froze labour rights laws passed by the former legislature.
"Labour unions...can certainly challenge the decision to freeze these labour law. The Democratic Party will certain render assistance," party spokesman Albert Ho said in a forum.
"For instance, I am a lawyer, I would give them free legal advise and free legal services," he added.

Other lawyers were also gearing up to challenge a law passed by the interim legislature that threatens to deport child illegal immigrants back to China even though they may have a theoretical legal right of abode here under the Basic Law.
A preliminary hearing takes place on Monday.
Activists have also decried proposals by Hong Kong chief executive Tung Chee-hwa on arrangements for the 1998 legislative polls.
For directly elected seats, Tung backs creation of a system of proportional representation in which the territory is divided into five geographical constituencies, each with multiple seats.
That contrasts with the arrangement in the last legislative election in 1995 when Hong Kong was divided into 20 smaller geographical constituencies, each with a single seat.
Democrats say such a change would reduce the chances of the Democratic Party, which won the largest number of seats in the 1995 election.
The plan would also replace individual votes with corporate votes for some indirectly elected seats, cutting the number of voters.

A survey commissioned by the South China Morning Post newspaper found only 26 percent of respondents favoured proportional representation, and more than 70 percent disagreed with the move to replace individual votes with corporate votes.

Tung's proposal also bans people with foreign passports from contesting the directly elected seats. Lau condemned the plan as "very unfair" and "very arbitrary", and threatened to mount a legal challenge to the arrangements should they become law.

Just one month after Tung took office, however, Hong Kong's 6.4 million people are giving him much higher support than before the handover. The latest opinion poll gave him a 78 percent satisfaction rating against 57 percent in June.

But 26 percent of Hong Kong people say they would rather be ruled by Britain than China, against 19 percent in June, while those preferring Beijing rule fell from 40 percent to 36 percent, the survey said.
